cells.tense: You are starting this out loud, and the people nearby can feel the current.
cells.ask: Pick the smallest real piece of this and start it where someone can see. Then tell that person plainly it's new and you don't know how it ends.
cells.core:
You're putting something into the world and not hiding that you're new at it. People feel that and lean in — they pick up on the difference between someone showing off and someone actually alight. And you can read a whole situation while you're standing in it, which means you start things in the right order. Those two together are rarer than the energy alone.

The balance isn't something you keep. The next thing this wants to feed is being able to cut through to the plain logic once the shine wears off and the work gets specific. So when it gets there, let the shine go and do the reasoning. The two together are what makes this hold.
cells.sheetLine: You're lit up and you can read the whole board at once.
cells.verb: Starting something new and letting the confidence show while it's still learning
cells.place: Standing back from the whole board without leaving the room

cells.tense: You are living in a Tuesday that hasn't arrived yet, bracing like it's already late.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you've been rehearsing the case for. Say it once, plainly, then stop talking and let the silence sit — no defending it after.
cells.core:
You make something, you're honestly lit about it, and it comes across because it's real. When this behavior is working, the spark does the talking and you let it. That's the whole trick, and you already have it.

What's happening instead is that the energy is going into a future version where it finally lands. So a conversation gets recruited into that — you're pushing the understanding ahead of the actual moment. The push is aimed at being received, and it's arriving as a pitch. The feeling of being behind is real to you. But the finish you're racing toward doesn't exist yet, and the rehearsing is eating the present the work actually needs.
cells.sheetLine: You're pressing the case instead of letting it land.

cells.tense: You set it down a while back and you're still standing where the thing was already finished.
cells.ask: Say out loud one true thing about how this actually is. Not what it should be — what's in front of you. Then let that be where you start from.
cells.core:
There's something you started once that came to a real finish, and you've stopped pointing at it. It's not that you can't read the pattern now — you can take in a whole situation from the outside — it's that the reading isn't moving you. Good observations fill the room and nothing gets started from them.

Don't push yourself to feel sparkling. Start small and material: water one thing, tidy one corner, take the next concrete step that doesn't need inspiration to begin. Doing that pulls the current back through. Reading a room gets easy again when the hands are already moving.

cells.tense: The radiance is already running and you're describing it like weather you didn't cause.
cells.ask: Name one thing you started or held steady this month, say the words 'I did that' out loud, and don't qualify it with luck.
cells.core:
You walk into a conversation carrying something, and the conversation shifts because you're in it. That's what this looks like when it's running clean — not loud, just present and steady enough that the room takes its cue. People follow because the confidence is real. And it's already happening.

What you don't do is claim it. You credit the situation, the timing, the group. But the confidence is coming from you — that's a lot closer to the front than where you're standing. The pattern that's hidden isn't your ability to read a room. It's who did the reading. You've been giving that away as just being perceptive.
cells.sheetLine: The radiance is yours. You've been calling it the room.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim in the draft: that the person is already reading the whole board at this seat, or already radiating. The record supports the capacity being present and its authorship being unattributed, but it does not support the person recognising themselves in that description, and the Too Little cell is most exposed: it may describe someone who simply has not developed the capacity rather than someone who has and is sitting behind it. The reader could reasonably say 'I don't see patterns, I just got through the week,' and the ask must still be useful then — naming one true thing about the situation, said out of the reading, does not require them to have read it whole or to be right. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line that congratulates them for a method I invented, so those are stripped.
